Avoid shared-memory bank conflicts by choosing layouts where warp threads do not repeatedly hit the same bank.  **Most impactful when:** there is spatial or temporal reuse within a thread block, such as tiled stencils, reductions, matrix-like access patterns, or repeated lookup of shared tables.### 3. Tune occupancy, but avoid chasing maximum occupancy blindlyUse block sizes that are multiples of 32; 128–256 threads per block are often good starting points on A100. Watch register use and shared-memory allocation because excessive use can reduce active warps per SM. Avoid register spilling, since spilled values go to local memory backed by DRAM. Use tools such as the CUDA Occupancy Calculator, `cudaOccupancyMaxPotentialBlockSize`, and Nsight Compute.  **Most impactful when:** latency hiding is poor, memory latency dominates, or register/shared-memory use limits active warps. Good occupancy reduces idle SM time and improves work completed per joule.### 4. Reduce warp divergenceRestructure branches so threads in the same warp follow the same path when possible. Replace short divergent branches with predication or branchless expressions, and group or sort inputs so similar work is processed by the same warps.  **Most impactful when:** branch paths are long, data-dependent, or highly irregular, causing warps to serialize multiple paths with inactive lanes.### 5. Fuse compatible kernelsCombine consecutive kernels that operate on the same data so intermediate results stay in registers or shared memory instead of being written to and reread from global memory. This also reduces kernel launch overhead.  **Most impactful when:** kernels are bandwidth-bound, operate elementwise or pipeline-style on the same arrays, and have compatible launch configurations and dependencies.### 6.
